newsitem.title: BELGIUM: City Bird aims to grab long-haul Brussels air traffic.
newsitem.headline: City Bird aims to grab long-haul Brussels air traffic.

text.p: Fledgling airline City Bird has mega ambitions to become the leading long-haul carrier from the capital of Europe, saying on Wednesday Brussels offered vast untapped potential for transatlantic traffic.
"I see City Bird becoming one of the main, if not the main long-haul airline flying from Brussels," City Bird president Victor Hasson told Reuters in an interview.
"There's the contract with (tour operator) NUR...there's Brussels, which is a desert when it comes to long-haul. It's the right time to give it a try," he said.

He said Belgian flag carrier Sabena should be ruled out as a long-haul carrier partly because it had focused on developing its European hub and passengers were not convinced of the quality of its code-sharing deal with U.S. carrier Delta Air.
"If we're successful, we'll have 10 times more trumps than Sabena, which is bogged down in problems with unions. We have fewer costs, we are more flexible," he said.
City Bird is 62.5-percent owned by Belgian hotels and leisure group City Hotels, which is also run by Hasson.
It will launch on March 27 with a starting capital of just $5 million but can bank on financial backing from City Hotels, whose previous adventure in aviation became an instant success.

Hasson launched a European regional carrier, EuroBelgian Airlines, in late 1991 with $1.5 million and sold 90 percent of it last year to British entrepreneur Richard Branson for $53 million. EBA now trades under Branson's Virgin Express brand.

City Hotels has said it has more than one billion francs ($29.6 million) in cash and is due to issue bonds worth another billion in the next few weeks. The new financing is earmarked for the company's hotels business.

Operating a McDonnell Douglas MD-11 aircraft, which is leased for 18 years, City Bird will offer, via leading Belgian tour operator NUR, flights from Brussels to the Dominican Republic, Cuba, Mexico and Jamaica.
Once it has a second MD-11 in June it will also run regular services to Miami, Orlando and Mexico, and to Los Angeles, San Francisco and New York.
Hasson said that NUR was filling 65 percent of the first plane but that the second would have to lure passengers from other airlines' scheduled services.

"The second is more risky...but I'm convinced that there are enough passengers to fill two flights a week to Los Angeles for example. It's just a matter of getting people to know the product," he said.
Asked why no-one else had tried to launch a long-haul carrier in Brussels, Hasson maintained there were no entrepeneurs in Belgium.
Hasson noted his contract with Branson stipulated he could not launch a rival European regional carrier.
Hasson played down the impact of soaring fuel prices and the dollar's rise on the new airline.
"Fuel was already high when we (announced) our tariffs and we're covered for the dollar," he said.

He said City Bird already signed a deal with Swissair, which has 49.5 percent of Sabena, for most of the maintenance, and that it planned deals with Sabena or Belgian Belgavia for handling and catering.
He said there was "good understanding" but no talks with Sabena about cooperating on routes.
